For too long, communities across this country have felt that investment flowed to the big cities while their high streets emptied and their bus routes were cut. This fund is a direct answer to that grievance. It puts money where people actually live, and it does so on the basis of bids developed by local councils, local businesses and local people who know their areas best. I want to be clear about how the fund will operate. Bids will be assessed against transparent criteria: the strength of the economic case, the deliverability of the project, and the extent to which it commands genuine local support, including the support of the local Member of Parliament. Priority will be given to those places most in need of regeneration, because levelling up cannot mean spreading resources thinly and evenly; it must mean concentrating effort where the gap is widest. Some Members opposite will say that this is too little, or that it does not compensate for other pressures on local government finance. I understand those concerns, and I do not dismiss them, but I would gently say that a fund of this scale, targeted in this way, is a substantial commitment by any historical standard. It sits alongside the towns fund, the shared prosperity fund and record investment in transport outside London. Taken together, these programmes represent the most serious attempt in a generation to change the economic geography of this country. I encourage every local authority represented in this House to work with its partners, to be ambitious in what it asks for, and to bring forward bids that will make a visible difference on the ground. The people we serve do not want warm words about regional inequality; they want cranes in the sky, shops reopening and buses that turn up. This fund will help to deliver exactly that.

Members will forgive a father's pride, but I mention Ozara today because she is the reason I want to speak about what kind of country we are building for the children who will inherit it. When she visits this place, she sees it with completely fresh eyes. She does not see partisanship or procedure; she sees a room where grown-ups are supposed to solve problems. I have often thought that if we conducted ourselves as though a four-year-old were watching—because, in truth, millions of them are—we might get more done and shout rather less. The issue before us today matters precisely because its consequences will land not on us but on her generation. The decisions we take on climate, on debt, on the affordability of housing and on the accessibility of education are all, in the end, promises we are making to children who cannot yet vote and cannot yet hold us to account. That is a profound responsibility, and it should discipline how we legislate. I want my daughter to grow up in a country where the career she dreams about—whether that is flying commercial aircraft or, heaven help her, standing in this chamber—is genuinely open to her, and open to every child regardless of the postal code they are born into or the income of their parents. That means investing early: in child care that families can actually afford, in schools that are properly resourced, and in communities where kids are safe. It also means fiscal honesty, because every dollar we borrow carelessly today is a dollar her generation must repay. I will support measures in this House that meet that test, and I will oppose those that fail it, whichever side proposes them. That is the standard Ozara would expect of me, and it is the standard I intend to keep.

Let me set out what we are doing. The United Kingdom remains one of the largest bilateral donors to the Syrian humanitarian response. Our funding supports food, clean water, medical care and education for millions of people inside Syria and in neighbouring countries—Jordan, Lebanon and Turkey—whose generosity in hosting refugees has been extraordinary and deserves our continued support. None of those conditions is currently met. We also continue to pursue accountability. The mechanisms gathering evidence of atrocities—the use of chemical weapons, the targeting of hospitals, the industrial-scale torture documented in the Caesar photographs—are painstaking, but they matter, because the day will come when those responsible face justice, and the record we help to preserve now will make that possible. I know the hon. Lady will say that the world's attention has moved on, and she is right to warn against that. Fatigue is the friend of impunity. So let me give her this assurance: we will maintain our humanitarian commitment, we will keep pressing for cross-border access at the Security Council, and we will not accept a settlement that simply rewards the regime for outlasting the conscience of the international community. The Syrian people deserve better than our forgetfulness, and while she and I are in this House, they will not have it.

someone who has spent a good part of my career arguing about buses, I make no apology for returning to them today, because buses are the workhorse of public transport and the mode on which the poorest in our communities most depend. The review that the combined authority is undertaking is welcome, but reviews do not carry passengers; services do. Over the past decade we have watched route after route withdrawn, evening and Sunday services pared back, and fares rise faster than wages. The people who pay the price are shift workers who cannot get home at night, young people who cannot take up apprenticeships, and older residents left isolated in villages that no longer have a service at all. Franchising offers us a genuine opportunity to change that. It allows the public to specify the network—the routes, the frequencies, the fares and the standards—and to reinvest revenue from busy corridors into the socially necessary services that a purely commercial operator will never run. I urge the combined authority to be bold in taking that path and not to be deterred by the inevitable resistance from incumbent operators. On active travel, I welcome the focus in the plan, but I would say gently that painted lines on busy roads are not infrastructure. If we want people to cycle, we need segregated routes that a parent would be happy for their child to use, and we need them joined up rather than stopping abruptly at the most dangerous junctions. Finally, on decarbonisation, the transition to a zero-emission fleet must come with investment in depots and charging, and it must protect the jobs of the drivers and engineers who keep the network moving. Done well, this plan can cut congestion, clean our air and reconnect communities that have been cut off for too long. I will support the authority in delivering it, and I will hold it to account if it falls short.

When a survivor stands before a classroom and rolls up their sleeve to show the number tattooed on their arm, no student who witnesses it can ever be persuaded that the Holocaust was exaggerated or invented. But we are losing those witnesses, year by year, and into the silence they leave behind step the deniers, the distorters and the trivialisers—people who claim the numbers were inflated, that the camps were something other than what they were, or who grotesquely compare public health measures to the persecution of the Jews. This is not fringe activity any more. It spreads through social media at a speed and scale that the survivors' generation could never have imagined, and studies of young people's knowledge show alarming gaps: significant numbers cannot say what Auschwitz was or how many Jews were murdered. Against that backdrop, the law we are considering does two essential things. First, it draws a clear line: wilful denial and distortion of the Holocaust, used as a vehicle for antisemitic hatred, is not legitimate historical debate and will not be treated as such. Second, and just as important, it affirms our collective responsibility for education—for ensuring that every student learns not only the facts of the Shoah but the process by which a civilised society descended into genocide: the propaganda, the scapegoating, the incremental stripping of rights, the silence of bystanders. I want to be clear that this law is not about criminalising honest scholarship or good-faith inquiry; historians have nothing to fear from it. It is aimed at those who lie about the murder of six million people in order to rehabilitate the ideology that murdered them. As the eyewitnesses leave us, the duty of witness passes to the law, to our schools and to us. We should accept that duty without hesitation.

He was a practical man—a farmer, a conservationist long before it was fashionable, and a champion of the skills and self-reliance that our upland communities embody. Through his patronage of countless organisations, agricultural societies among them, he showed a genuine and knowledgeable interest in farming that endeared him to many of my constituents. But perhaps his greatest legacy, and the one that will endure longest in Penrith and The Border as everywhere else, is the Duke of Edinburgh's Award. Millions of young people across this country and the Commonwealth have hiked across our fells, camped in our valleys and discovered reserves of resilience they did not know they had, because of a scheme he founded in 1956 and championed all his life. Young people in my constituency are among them, and the confidence and character the award has given them is a living memorial that no statue could match. He was famously impatient with fuss, direct to the point of bluntness, and utterly allergic to self-importance—qualities that Cumbrians recognise and admire. He walked two paces behind the Queen for 73 years, and in doing so he showed that there is profound strength in service, and profound dignity in supporting another's duty. On behalf of my constituents, I offer Her Majesty and the royal family our deepest condolences. May he rest in peace, and may his example of duty, service and quiet strength endure.

Every study we have, and more importantly every elder and every community leader, tells us the same thing: outcomes improve when indigenous communities control the services that shape their lives—their child welfare, their education, their health care, their justice. That is what real reconciliation looks like: not a moment of ceremony, but a transfer of decision-making. So I ask members on all sides, when this bill comes to a vote, to think about a young man sitting in a room full of well-meaning voices, holding a pain that none of them could see. We can keep building rooms like that, or we can finally build institutions where his voice is not an afterthought but the starting point. I know which country I want to leave to him.

The reality check I want to focus on is this: the measures announced yesterday will only work if they are matched by support that makes compliance possible. It is no good telling people to isolate if they cannot afford to miss a shift. The evidence is clear that isolation rates are lowest among those who can least afford to stay at home, and that is not a failure of public spirit; it is a failure of policy. So I say to Ministers: fix sick pay, extend the isolation payments, and stop pretending that a £500 payment with a restrictive eligibility test reaches the people who need it. The second reality is about the health service. We came into this crisis with waiting lists already at record levels and tens of thousands of staff vacancies. The backlog now building up—the cancelled operations, the delayed diagnoses, the cancer patients whose treatment has been pushed back—will be with us for years, and we need an honest, funded recovery plan, not a slogan. The third reality concerns the vaccine. The programme is going well and everyone involved deserves enormous credit, but vaccination is a race against transmission, and every week of high prevalence is another week in which new variants can emerge. That argues for caution in easing restrictions, however weary we all are, and for finally securing our borders against importation with a comprehensive quarantine policy rather than the half-measures we have seen. I welcome the realism that broke out yesterday. My plea is that it should not be a moment but a habit. If the Government level with the public, put support alongside every restriction, and plan for recovery now, they will have my support. What none of us can afford is a fourth round of the same mistakes.

This is not a utopian scheme that requires new institutions or heroic assumptions; it is a practical adjustment to an existing tax that everyone, including successive Chancellors, admits is broken. Let me spell out why the current system fails. Business rates are charged on the rateable value of premises, which means a retailer with a shop on the high street pays substantially more, relative to turnover, than an online warehouse on the edge of town. We are, in effect, taxing the very presence on the high street that every party in this House says it wants to preserve, while lightly taxing the distribution model that is hollowing it out. No one designed that outcome; it is an accident of a tax created for a different economy, but the effect is the same as if we had set out deliberately to disadvantage our town centres. Our report proposes rebalancing the burden, coupled with more frequent revaluations so that bills track economic reality rather than lagging years behind it, and relief that is automatic rather than dependent on annual Treasury announcements that leave businesses unable to plan. I stress again the word deliverable. We took evidence from the retail sector, from small business federations, from local authorities and from the Treasury itself, and nothing we heard suggested that these reforms are technically infeasible. What has been missing is not capability but will—the will to take on a reform that has losers as well as winners, and to stop treating each Budget's temporary relief as a substitute for structural change. I hope the Minister, when he responds, will not simply list the reliefs already granted, welcome though they are, but engage with the central point: the system itself needs reform, the reform is doable, and the time to do it is now.

I have met business organisations, hauliers, manufacturers and farmers from across Northern Ireland, and their message is remarkably uniform: they are not interested in constitutional theology; they are interested in whether their lorries move, whether their supply chains function, and whether they can sell to their biggest market—Great Britain—without friction, cost and paperwork that their competitors do not face. Northern Ireland's businesses sell more to Great Britain than to Ireland, the rest of the EU and the rest of the world combined. That is not a political claim; it is a statistical fact, and any arrangement that impedes that trade strikes at the foundation of Northern Ireland's economy. This Bill guarantees unfettered access in law, and it does so while maintaining our commitments to no hard border on the island of Ireland and to the protection of the Belfast agreement in all its dimensions. Members opposite ask about the rhetoric surrounding the Bill, and I have given my answer: I will deal with the text, not the commentary. The text provides certainty. It tells a manufacturer in Ballymena or a food producer in Fermanagh that their goods will continue to flow to customers in Liverpool and Glasgow without new barriers erected in either direction. It gives businesses the confidence to invest, to hire and to plan beyond the next quarter—confidence that has been in desperately short supply over the past four years. Of course, legislation alone does not complete the task. The detailed implementation, the guidance and the systems at ports must all work in practice, and I will hold the Government to account on every element of that delivery. But the starting point is legal certainty, and that is what this Bill delivers. Businesses have asked for it; we should give it to them.

Let us be honest about the scale of what remains to be done. People with disabilities in this country are more likely to live in poverty, less likely to be in employment, and more likely to face barriers in housing, transport and education than almost anywhere else in Europe. The cost of disability—the additional, unavoidable expense of simply living with a disability—is estimated at thousands of euro a year, yet our income supports take no adequate account of it. Ratifying the convention obliges us to confront these facts, not to file them away. I want to highlight three priorities. First, the optional protocol must be ratified without further delay, because a convention without a complaints mechanism asks citizens to trust that the State will mark its own homework. Second, we need a personalised budgets model that gives people with disabilities genuine control over the supports they receive, rather than obliging them to fit their lives around services designed for administrative convenience. Third, we must end the scandal of young people with disabilities living in nursing homes because no appropriate accommodation exists—there are hundreds of them, and every one represents a failure of planning and of will. I acknowledge that progress has been made and that many officials and Ministers have worked in good faith, but people with disabilities have been asked to be patient for decades, through strategy after strategy and review after review. Patience is not a policy. The convention we ratify today sets out rights—to independent living, to education, to work, to participation in public life—and rights are not aspirations to be delivered when resources allow; they are entitlements to be vindicated. I will judge the Government not by today's welcome words but by the budgets, the timelines and the delivery that follow.

The petitioners ask that the Government act on the science, transition open-net pen fish farms out of the migratory routes of wild Pacific salmon, and invest seriously in habitat restoration before it is too late. Mr. Speaker, the numbers speak for themselves. Runs that once returned in the millions now return in the thousands. Last year, some rivers in British Columbia saw historic lows, and communities that have fished those waters for generations—first nations communities above all, whose rights and cultures are inseparable from the salmon—watched empty rivers where their grandparents hauled in abundance. This is not only an environmental tragedy; it is an economic and cultural one. Coastal communities depend on salmon for jobs in fishing, processing and tourism. First nations depend on salmon for food security and for the continuity of practices that predate this country by millennia. The southern resident killer whales, an icon of our coast, are starving in part because the chinook they depend on are disappearing. The causes are multiple—warming waters, habitat destruction, predation, harvest pressure—and the petitioners do not pretend there is a single villain. But where the science identifies risks we can control, such as the transfer of pathogens and parasites from farmed to wild fish, we have a duty to act with precaution rather than wait for certainty that will arrive only after the collapse is irreversible. The petitioners therefore call for a clear, funded timeline for the transition to closed containment, expanded habitat restoration through the salmon strategy, and co-management with first nations whose knowledge of these runs is unmatched. I am proud to table this petition on their behalf, and I urge the Government to respond not with process, but with action commensurate with the emergency.

I want to put the broader picture before the House, because Deputies are proposing further reductions as though the Exchequer were a bottomless well. The reductions we introduced were among the most significant ever applied to excise on fuel, and they came at a very substantial cost to the Exchequer—hundreds of millions of euro on a full-year basis—at the same time as we were funding supports for households on electricity costs, increases in the fuel allowance and a range of other cost-of-living measures. Every further cent of reduction costs millions more, and it is worth being honest that a large portion of any excise cut can be absorbed into the retail margin rather than passed to the motorist at the pump. We saw evidence of exactly that pattern in the weeks after previous reductions, which is why the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission has been asked to monitor pricing closely. There is also a European dimension that Deputies sometimes wave away: the energy tax directive sets minimum rates below which we cannot lawfully go, and we are now close to those floors for some fuels. Beyond the legal constraint lies a policy one. We have committed, across parties in this House, to carbon budgets and to a trajectory on emissions. I understand completely the pressure on rural households and on hauliers, for whom there is no realistic alternative to the car or the truck today, and that is precisely why supports are targeted at them. But a general race to the bottom on fuel taxation would benefit the largest consumers most, would blow a hole in the public finances we need for those targeted supports, and would do nothing about the underlying cause, which is a war-driven spike in international prices. I will keep the measures under review, as I have said, and if the situation deteriorates further the Government will respond, as we have responded at every point in this crisis.

new clause would simply require the Government to publish a proper assessment of the tax gap and of the effectiveness of their anti-avoidance measures, and I struggle to see how any Member could object to transparency of that kind. If the Government are as confident in their record as they claim, an independent assessment will vindicate them; if they are not, the public deserve to know. The scale of what we are discussing should concentrate minds. The tax gap runs to tens of billions of pounds every year—money that should be funding our schools, our hospitals and our social security system, sitting instead in offshore structures and creative accounting schemes. And this is only the gap that HMRC itself estimates; independent analysts believe the true figure, once profit shifting by multinationals is properly counted, is considerably higher. Meanwhile, HMRC's resources for enforcement have been cut, its offices closed and its experienced compliance staff lost, at exactly the moment when the complexity of avoidance schemes is increasing. Every pound spent on compliance returns many times its cost, so cutting enforcement is not saving; it is a false economy of the most self-defeating kind. Scotland's position is straightforward: we did not choose the tax system we live under in reserved matters, and where we have had powers—on income tax, on land transactions—we have used them progressively and, dare I say, competently. The revelations in successive leaks, from Panama to Pandora, showed how deeply the UK's overseas territories and Crown dependencies are embedded in the global avoidance industry, and yet registers of beneficial ownership have been delayed year after year. So I say to the Minister: accept our new clause, publish the analysis, properly resource HMRC, and bring forward the transparency measures that have been promised since 2016. If the Government will not act with the powers they hoard at Westminster, they should not be surprised that we conclude those powers would be better exercised elsewhere.

That is not a point of nationalist pride; it is a lesson in how public services work best—locally rooted, publicly run and democratically accountable. The recovery must repay that debt. I walked out of that branch with a bank book, and every lodgement and withdrawal for years afterwards was written down where I could see it, understand it and question it. I mention that not out of nostalgia—though I confess to some—but because it goes to the heart of what we are debating: access. For my mother's generation and for many of my constituents today, banking is not an app; it is a counter, a familiar face and a conversation. When banks close their branches, as they have done at an extraordinary rate across Northern Ireland, they do not merely inconvenience those customers; they exclude them. Consider who is left behind. The elderly gentleman who has never used the internet and does not intend to start now. The small shopkeeper who needs to lodge cash takings and must now drive twenty miles to do it, carrying that cash with all the risk that entails. The community group whose treasurer cannot get change for the weekend's events. Rural communities where broadband is patchy at best, so the promised digital alternative is no alternative at all. The banks tell us that footfall is falling and that customers have moved online, and for many that is true. But the customers who remain dependent on branches are precisely those with the fewest alternatives, and a civilised banking system does not abandon its least profitable customers; it serves them, because access to cash and to basic banking is not a luxury product—it is essential infrastructure, like the post office and the road. So I support the measures before us to protect access to cash and to require proper assessment before the last branch in a town closes. I would go further and support shared banking hubs in every town that loses its branches. My mother taught me that a bank account was a serious thing, a foundation for a working life. We should legislate as though we still believe that.

The House should understand what makes Luton's case exceptional. For decades, the dividend from the airport—owned by the council on behalf of the people of Luton—has funded services and supported the voluntary sector across our town. It is a model that has been praised across the political spectrum: a municipally owned asset generating tens of millions of pounds for the public good. But when air travel collapsed in the pandemic, that income collapsed with it, at the very moment when demand for council services was surging. Luton faces a shortfall running to tens of millions of pounds through no fault of its own—not through mismanagement, not through profligacy, but because the town did the responsible thing and built its finances on a productive asset that a global pandemic then grounded. At the start of this crisis, the Secretary of State told councils to do whatever it takes and promised that the Government would stand behind them. Luton took that promise at face value. Yet the support provided so far covers only a fraction of the losses, and the Government's scheme for lost sales, fees and charges explicitly excludes commercial income of exactly the kind Luton depends on. The consequence is that the council has been forced into an emergency budget, with cuts of millions of pounds to services that our residents—among the hardest hit by the virus itself—rely on. The petitioners therefore request that the House urge the Government to honour the commitment that was made: to provide Luton Council with the support necessary to offset its losses, so that the people of Luton do not pay twice for this pandemic—once in their health and livelihoods, and again in the loss of the local services they need most. I accept fully that clinical standards matter and that not every hospital can provide every specialty. Nobody is arguing for unsafe services. But the answer to a staffing or resourcing problem in a regional hospital cannot forever be to remove the service rather than fix the problem. We have seen that pattern too many times: a service is allowed to wither through recruitment freezes and underinvestment, and then its very weakness is cited as the justification for closing it. It is a self-fulfilling prophecy dressed up as clinical judgment. So I ask the Minister to do three things: publish in full the plans for the hospital so the community can see them; give a binding commitment that no service will be withdrawn without a genuine alternative in place and functioning first; and invest in the recruitment and retention measures needed to make the hospital sustainable. The people of the region have marched, petitioned and pleaded. They deserve certainty, and I will not rest until they have it.

What I want to see—and what I believe every Member of this House wants to see—is the restoration of the Executive and the Assembly, so that decisions about health, education and the economy in Northern Ireland are taken by locally elected Ministers accountable to local people. We proposed exactly what the House sees today: a reduced complement, physical distancing, all public health guidance respected—the same accommodations that grocery stores, pharmacies and countless workplaces have made. If a supermarket in Winnipeg can figure out how to operate safely, surely the House of Commons, with all its resources, can do the same. What the government prefers instead is a daily press conference from a podium, where the Prime Minister takes the questions he wishes to take, for as long as he wishes to take them, with no order paper questions, no committees with full powers, and no ability for members to hold ministers to account on behalf of their constituents. A press conference is not a Parliament. Accountability is not an inconvenience to be suspended in hard times; hard times are precisely when accountability matters most, because that is when the most money is spent, the most power is concentrated and the most mistakes are made. Every dollar of emergency spending deserves scrutiny not because we assume bad faith, but because scrutiny is how a democracy catches errors before they become scandals. So I ask the government House leader again: why will this government not let Parliament do its job?

We heard in evidence that simply modernising those systems would pay for itself within a few years through reduced running costs and error rates—yet the investment is repeatedly deferred because the annual funding round cannot accommodate a commitment of that length. This is a false economy repeated across government, but here its effects fall on some of the most vulnerable people in the country, who depend on payments arriving accurately and on time. So the Committee's recommendation is clear: the Treasury should agree a multi-year settlement tied to a published modernisation plan, with milestones that this House can scrutinise. In return, the Department must be honest about its delivery record, because ambitious IT programmes in this area have gone wrong before, and the lessons of those failures—overambition, weak contract management, big-bang cutovers instead of incremental change—are well documented and must be applied. I do not underestimate the difficulty. But the choice before us is not between spending and not spending; it is between spending deliberately on a system that works and spending endlessly on propping up one that does not. Ashling was a young woman with everything before her—a talented musician, a teacher adored by the children in her class—and she was killed in daylight, doing something as ordinary and as innocent as going for a run along a canal. That knowledge, shared and unspoken, is an indictment of us all. So what must we do to ensure this conversation endures? First, we must fund the response properly. Zero tolerance as a slogan costs nothing; refuges, court supports, and perpetrator programmes cost money, and the strategy must come with multi-annual funding, not aspirational figures. There are still counties in this State without a single refuge place, years after we committed to the Istanbul convention. That is a source of shame. Second, education: consent and respectful relationships must be taught properly in every school, because the attitudes that end in violence begin in the everyday disrespect that too often goes unchallenged, in classrooms, in workplaces and online. Third, justice: women who report domestic and sexual violence still face delays, retraumatising procedures and attrition rates that tell perpetrators the odds are on their side. Court delays must be cut and specialist training made universal. Finally, this cannot be women's work alone. It was a man who killed Ashling Murphy, and it is men—all of us—who must challenge the misogyny in our midst, in our friend groups and in ourselves. And what has this bypassing achieved? The evidence is before us: a large share of the permissions granted through fast-track processes have ended up in judicial review, precisely because cutting the public out at the front door invites them to seek justice at the back door. Litigation is not a sign of a vexatious public; it is the symptom of a planning system that has stopped listening. Nor, crucially, has it delivered homes: vast numbers of fast-track permissions remain unbuilt while land values are banked. So we have sacrificed trust and gained neither speed nor supply. I say to the Minister: the answer to the housing emergency is not less democracy but better planning—plan-led development, properly resourced planning departments, decisions made at the level closest to the people affected, and an end to the fiction that public participation is the enemy of delivery. Communities are not obstacles to be managed. They are the reason planning exists at all, and any system that forgets that will find, as this one has, that trust once squandered is very hard to win back.

That is precisely the point I want the House to grasp: the constitutional monarch's duties are not ornamental. The conventions that require the sovereign to act on the advice of Ministers, to remain scrupulously above party, and to embody continuity rather than opinion are load-bearing walls of our constitution, and they held in the twentieth century because the individuals concerned understood and honoured them. George VI, thrust unprepared onto the throne by his brother's abdication, understood them profoundly; his steadiness, and that of Queen Elizabeth, gave Churchill's Government a foundation of legitimacy at the moment of maximum national peril. Edward VIII, by contrast, had already shown as king a willingness to blur the line between personal inclination and public duty, and his subsequent conduct—the flirtations with regimes that wished this country ill—suggests how differently events might have unfolded had he remained. Counterfactual history is a parlour game, but it is a useful one, because it reminds us that institutions do not run on autopilot. They run on the character of the people within them and on the willingness of politicians to respect boundaries even when crossing them would be convenient. That is the lesson I draw for the matter before us today. When we legislate on constitutional questions, we are not merely arranging machinery; we are setting expectations for behaviour in crises we cannot foresee. We should therefore legislate with humility, preserving the conventions that have proven themselves under the severest tests, and resisting the temptation to treat as obsolete the safeguards whose value is invisible precisely because they have worked. The abdication crisis was resolved in weeks because the institutions around the Crown functioned; the counterexample I have sketched shows what was at stake if they had not. We are custodians of that same inheritance, and we should hand it on undamaged.

Third, the funding must be identified in the Estimates, because a plan without a budget line is a press release. The sums involved here are modest by the standards of Government spending, and the cost of inaction—borne in other budgets, in health, in education supports, in family breakdown—almost certainly exceeds the cost of acting. When we run structural deficits in years of growth, we are making a claim on the earnings of people too young to vote and people not yet born, without their consent and without their knowledge. There are times when borrowing is right—recessions, emergencies, investments that will yield returns for the very generations who help pay for them—but a habit of financing today's consumption with tomorrow's taxes fails the sustainability test in exactly the way that exhausting a fishery or degrading a watershed fails it. The principle is identical: do not take from the future what you are unwilling to pay for in the present. Consider our social programs. A pension system, a health system, a public service—each is an intergenerational compact, sustainable only if each generation contributes on terms that leave the system sound for the next. When we defer maintenance, hide liabilities off the books or promise benefits without funding them, we are not being generous; we are being generous with other people's money, specifically our children's. And consider our institutions. Trust in parliaments, courts and elections is itself a form of capital, accumulated over generations and easily squandered within one. Every time we degrade norms for short-term partisan advantage, we draw down an account we did not fill. So I propose a simple discipline for this chamber: that we ask of every significant measure the sustainability question—what does this do to the options, the resources and the institutions available to those who come after us? Some measures before us this session pass that test handsomely, and I will support them. Others fail it, and I will say so regardless of which party proposes them. Environmental sustainability taught us to see the future as a stakeholder. It is time our fiscal and institutional debates learned the same lesson, because the generations to come will inherit every choice we make in this place, and they are not here to object.

The Holocaust was perpetrated by ordinary people, permitted by ordinary people, and, in the rescues that pierced the darkness, resisted by ordinary people. We in this House are ordinary people with an extraordinary platform. A system that catches a threat at the last line of defence is not a system that is working; it is a system that got lucky, and the difference matters enormously. The alert we are discussing succeeded because dedicated professionals intervened, and I join the Home Secretary in paying tribute to them. But the question this House must ask is why the earlier lines of defence did not hold—why the individual concerned was able to progress as far as they did before detection, what information was available at earlier stages, and whether that information was shared between the agencies and authorities that each held a piece of the picture. If that pattern is present here—and the House cannot yet know, which is itself part of the problem—then celebrating the final interception risks entrenching precisely the complacency that reviews have warned against. So I put three specific questions to the Home Secretary. First, will she commission an independent, end-to-end review of this case, covering every agency involved, with findings published to the maximum extent that security allows? Second, will she tell the House whether the information-sharing recommendations from previous reviews have been implemented in full—not accepted in principle, but implemented, with dates? Third, will she ensure that the resourcing of the earlier, less visible layers of the system—local policing, referral mechanisms, the caseworkers who assess risk long before a crisis—matches the investment we rightly make in the final defences? The public's safety depends not on the drama of the last-minute save but on the quiet competence of everything that should happen before it. I hope the Home Secretary will take these questions in the constructive spirit in which they are asked, because on this, of all subjects, the House works best when it works together.

The system is failing at both ends: the State pays among the highest prices in Europe for many medicines, yet Irish patients are among the last in western Europe to get access to new therapies. For a patient with months to live, a two-year process is not a delay; it is a refusal dressed in procedure. Clinicians know it, patients know it, and the campaign groups who come to our clinics and to the gates of this House know it best of all. Reform requires several things. The assessment process needs statutory timelines with public reporting against them, so that drift has a cost. The HSE needs the analytical resources to conduct assessments quickly and to negotiate from strength, including access to the real cost-effectiveness data the current approach obscures. We should make far greater use of joint procurement with other small and medium-sized European states, through the BeNeLuxA initiative and similar arrangements, because our negotiating position alone will always be weak against global companies. And there must be a transparent early-access mechanism for medicines addressing unmet need, with managed-access agreements that share risk between the State and industry while data matures. None of this is radical; all of it operates elsewhere. What is missing is the decision to do it, and every month of delay is measured out in the lives of patients who did nothing wrong except fall ill in the wrong country.

3:27 tells us, "A leader who lacks judgment is also a great oppressor, but the one who hates unjust gain will prolong his days." Her late Majesty's days were long indeed, and I believe the scriptures give us the reason: she led with judgment, she sought no gain for herself, and she shepherded her people with exactly that integrity of heart. Consider what her seven decades of service contained. She came to the throne a young woman of twenty-five, in a world of rationing and rebuilding, and she departed it in an age she could scarcely have imagined at her coronation. Fifteen Prime Ministers served her. Empires dissolved, a Commonwealth of free nations grew in their place, and through every convulsion—wars, recessions, the transformation of society itself—she remained what she had promised to be on her twenty-first birthday, when she declared that her whole life, whether it be long or short, would be devoted to our service. She kept that vow to her final days, discharging her duties with the same diligence in her tenth decade as in her third. That is covenant faithfulness of a kind our age has almost forgotten. Her faith was not ornamental. In her Christmas broadcasts, the one moment each year when she spoke in her own words rather than on advice, she returned again and again to her trust in God and to the example of Christ the servant king. She understood that the crown she wore pointed beyond itself, and that authority is given for service, not for self. In an era of leaders who grasp, she gave; in an era of noise, she kept counsel; in an era that celebrates the self, she poured hers out for others. The throne has passed, as she would have wished, in peace and good order. Our prayers are with the King and with all the royal family in their grief. And our gratitude—the gratitude of this place and of millions—goes with her. Well done, good and faithful servant. May she rest in peace and rise in glory.

Powers that bypass the ordinary architecture of criminal justice carry a cost to be justified anew each year, never assumed. I say to hon. It means the freeports programme creating hubs for trade and investment. It means the biggest rail investment outside London for a generation. It means moving thousands of civil service jobs out of Whitehall, so that policy is made by people who live in the communities it affects. It means investment in skills—the lifetime skills guarantee, the institutes of technology—so that opportunity means more than a job at the distribution shed on the ring road; it means careers, in industries with a future. And it means backing the sectors where Britain can lead the world: offshore wind in the north-east, life sciences in the golden triangle and beyond, advanced manufacturing in the midlands. My hon. Friend's constituency demonstrates what happens when national strategy meets local leadership: jobs created, investment attracted, and—just as important—pride restored. Because this agenda was never only about economics. It is about people feeling that where they live matters, that they do not have to move away to get on, and that the country's success includes them. That is the basic bargain of a modern republic: what you know, not who you know. Every young person who studies for years and prepares diligently for a public competition is entitled to believe the system is straight. Every public servant who was promoted on merit is insulted by the suggestion that the rules are for some and not for others. And every citizen who is asked to trust the State—with their taxes, their data, their children's education—has that trust chipped away when they see the State's own rules bent at the top. If the appointment could have survived an open competition, an open competition should have been held. That is the simple principle at the heart of this bill: informed consumers make better choices, and better choices discipline providers in a way no regulator ever could. Right now, the information asymmetry is almost total. Canadians sign contracts drafted by teams of corporate lawyers, filled with terms that shift beneath their feet: introductory rates that quietly expire, fees buried on page thirty, service levels promised in the advertisement and disclaimed in the fine print. When the bill arrives and it is higher than promised, when the speed delivered is a fraction of the speed advertised, the consumer discovers that the burden of proof, the burden of complaint and the burden of switching all fall on them. Companies have calculated, quite rationally, that confusion is profitable. Clarity, mandated and standardized, changes that calculation. When every provider must disclose the same information, in the same format, measured the same way, comparison becomes possible—and comparison is the engine of competition. We have seen this work in other jurisdictions and other sectors: standardized disclosure for financial products, for energy contracts, for food labelling. Nobody today would accept groceries without ingredient lists, yet we accept telecommunications and financial services—products most families spend more on than food some months—sold in a fog. Members opposite say the industry will comply reluctantly, that there will be costs. Of course there will be modest compliance costs, and I note the companies predicting ruin here made identical predictions about every previous consumer protection measure, all of which they absorbed while remaining among the most profitable firms in the country. The question for this House is not whether disclosure is convenient for providers; it is whether Canadians are entitled to know what they are buying before they buy it. I say they are. Honest businesses have nothing to fear from informed customers—indeed, they will gain market share from the dishonest ones. That is the whole point, and it is why I urge every member to support this bill.

This legislation would eliminate mandatory minimum penalties for a series of offences, including offences committed with firearms, and would expand the use of conditional sentences—house arrest—for crimes that my constituents would be astonished to learn could be served from a living room couch. The government presents this as criminal justice reform. These are not administrative offences or crimes of poverty; they are violent crimes that terrorize communities, and this bill removes the mandatory prison sentences attached to them—at the very moment when Canadian cities are experiencing a surge in gun violence, and when police chiefs across the country tell us that a small number of repeat violent offenders are responsible for a wildly disproportionate share of it. What message does this send to those offenders? And what message does it send to their victims? If the government's concern is over-incarceration, the evidence tells us where to act: bail reform done right, investment in mental health and addiction treatment, diversion for genuinely non-violent offenders, and support for indigenous justice programs—measures we could support. My constituents want a justice system that is fair, and they also want one that protects them. Those goals are not in tension; this bill, unfortunately, serves neither. I will be opposing it, and I urge the government to go back and separate the reforms worth making from the risks not worth taking.

Credibility is a currency, and currencies are for spending. That leads to my third idea: climate finance. But end-of-life care, which every single one of us will need in some form, is left to the generosity of communities—generosity that is real and moving, but which fluctuates with the economy and is distributed unevenly, so that the quality of your death can depend on the fundraising capacity of your county. The demographic facts are not in dispute—our population is ageing, and demand for palliative care will rise steeply over the next two decades. So I am asking the Minister for three commitments: a move to full core funding of hospice services on a multi-annual basis, so that no hospice depends on charity for its essential operations; investment in community palliative care teams to make death at home a genuine option in every county, not just some; and a workforce plan for palliative medicine and nursing to meet the demand we know is coming. How a society treats its dying is a measure of its decency. Ours is decent in spirit; it is time the funding matched.

Consider what powers the CBSA holds. Its officers can detain people, search people, arrest people. They carry firearms. They can hold non-citizens—including, until recently, children—in detention indefinitely, since immigration detention in Canada has no statutory time limit. These are among the most intrusive powers the state possesses, powers we rightly insist be checked wherever else they appear: the RCMP has a review commission, CSIS has independent review, municipal police forces answer to oversight boards. Yet the agency that exercises these powers over the most vulnerable people in our system—people who often do not speak our languages, do not know our laws and have no community to advocate for them—answers, in effect, only to itself. When someone dies in CBSA custody, the investigation is not conducted by an independent body with a public mandate; families wait years for answers that often never come, and the recommendations that do emerge from inquests have no enforcement behind them. Fifteen deaths since 2000 is fifteen too many, and the woman I mentioned—held in a maximum security provincial prison, though she was convicted of nothing, accused of no crime, detained purely on immigration grounds—should weigh on the conscience of this chamber. Immigration detention is administrative detention; that we house it in penitentiaries at all should trouble us deeply. The legislation before us would finally establish an independent review and complaints body for the CBSA, and I support it. But I urge members to strengthen it: the body must have the power to initiate its own investigations, not merely respond to complaints; it must have full access to detention facilities; and its recommendations must be answered publicly. Oversight is not an insult to the many border officers who do their jobs honourably; it is the ordinary architecture of accountability in a free country, and the CBSA has gone without it for far too long.

Consider the journey of Government policy on antigen tests. First they were dangerous; the public, we were told, could not be trusted to use them or understand the results. Then they were permissible in certain workplaces. Then they were advisable in some circumstances but not others, according to guidance that changed by the week. Now, at last, they are recommended—but at seven or eight euro a test in the shops, a family of five doing the twice-weekly testing that public health advice suggests faces a bill of hundreds of euro a month. In Britain they have been free for months. In Germany they cost less than a euro at the supermarket. Only here is a basic public health tool priced like a small luxury, and the result is exactly what anyone would predict: testing follows income, and the virus does not. So the Government's position amounts to this: we ask people to take personal responsibility while pricing the tools of personal responsibility beyond many households. Meanwhile PCR capacity is swamped, people queue for days for appointments, and infectious individuals circulate while they wait. The fix is neither complicated nor unaffordable, and the State's own advisers recommended it: free or heavily subsidised antigen tests, distributed through pharmacies, schools and workplaces, accompanied by clear communication about how and when to use them and what to do with a positive result. The cost is a fraction of what a single week of additional restrictions costs the Exchequer, never mind the economy. I ask the Minister to stop treating antigen testing as a concession to be made grudgingly and start treating it as the frontline defence it is. Every other comparable country has managed this. Our people deserve the same.

assessment, done seriously, before harm occurs—not content moderation done frantically, after the harm has gone viral. If the largest, richest, most technically sophisticated companies on earth cannot tell a parliamentary committee what risks their own systems create, who is exposed to those risks and what they are doing to mitigate them, then self-regulation has failed by its own chosen measure, and the case for this legislation makes itself. Let me explain why risk assessment is the right foundation. We regulate every other industry whose products can harm at scale in exactly this way. We do not wait for the bridge to collapse and then moderate the rubble; we require the engineering assessment before the bridge opens. We do not respond to contaminated food solely with recalls; we require hazard analysis in the production process. Yet platforms whose recommendation systems shape what billions of people—including millions of children—see every day have never been required to ask, systematically and answerably: what could this system do to the people who use it? Who might it push towards self-harm content, towards fraud, towards radicalisation? The companies possess this information, or could; their entire business is measurement. What they have lacked is any obligation to look, and any consequence for not looking. That is what the duty in this Bill changes, and it is why the lawful but harmful category, so often caricatured, matters. Nobody is asking platforms to criminalise legal speech. We are asking them to understand their own machines: to assess how design choices—autoplay, algorithmic amplification, frictionless sharing—turn individually lawful content into cumulative harm, the way a thousand individually legal posts about weight loss become, curated by an algorithm into a teenager's feed, something no parent would permit through the front door. Risk assessment, transparency about the findings, and accountability to an independent regulator with real powers: that is the architecture. The search companies' failure at the first hurdle is not a reason to lower the hurdle. It is the proof of why Parliament must set it.

I am confident of how that conversation ends, because I have had it on the doorsteps and the right hon. Gentleman's colleagues, in their more candid moments, know it too. Let us be precise about what this legislation does and does not do. The right to protest—to march, to assemble, to speak, to make a nuisance of oneself in the honourable tradition of British dissent—remains fully protected, as it must in any free country. Nothing in these measures prevents a single peaceful demonstration. What the measures address is a deliberate strategy, openly advertised by its practitioners, of imposing maximum disruption on the maximum number of ordinary people: gluing themselves to motorways, tunnelling under railways, blockading fuel depots and presses—tactics designed not to persuade fellow citizens but to hold them hostage. The public understand the difference between protest and sabotage even where the party opposite affects not to. When a nurse cannot get to her shift, when a father misses a funeral, when small businesses lose days of trade, the people responsible are not speaking truth to power; they are trampling on their neighbours, who have rights too. Hard-working people have been remarkably patient, and their patience has been repaid with contempt from protesters who boast about their arrests and return the next morning. The police asked for clearer powers to deal with these tactics; this Bill provides them, with judicial oversight and with the thresholds set out plainly on the face of the legislation. So the choice before the House is not liberty versus order; it is whether the law will protect the everyday freedoms of the many against the calculated obstruction of the few. I know where the Government stand, I know where the public stand, and the Opposition are welcome to explain, at length, why they stand somewhere else.

Prevention on the French coast is the humane point of intervention as well as the practical one, and I want to set out for the House how we are strengthening it. Under the agreement we have reached, the number of French officers patrolling the beaches will increase substantially, supported by UK-funded surveillance technology—drones, night-vision equipment and vehicle support—that extends coverage along an enormous and difficult coastline. Every crossing prevented on the beach is a family not put at risk in the world's busiest shipping lane, and it is revenue denied to those gangs. But I have never pretended to the House that enforcement alone is the answer, and I will not pretend it today. The equation changes only when the model of the smugglers is broken from both ends, which is why safe and legal routes matter—our resettlement schemes, the family reunion provisions—and why cooperation with France and with partners further upstream, along the whole migration route, is being deepened. It is also why the asylum system itself must be reformed, so that claims are decided quickly and fairly: swift protection for those who need it, and swift return for those with no right to be here, because a system where a claim takes years serves nobody except the gangs whose sales pitch depends on it. There is no single lever and no overnight solution, and anyone who offers the House one is not being straight. But the direction is clear: smash the gangs, prevent the crossings at the beaches, protect the genuinely vulnerable, and restore order and public confidence to a system that needs both.

I want this Chamber to learn the actual lesson of the last decade before we repeat its worst mistake. Austerity after the financial crash was presented as arithmetic, as though there were no choice involved. But it was a choice—a choice to balance the books on public services and social protection rather than on wealth; and we can now audit its results. It gave us the hollowed-out health service whose fragility this pandemic has so brutally exposed. It gave us a housing emergency, because the State stopped building precisely when building was cheapest. It gave us a lost decade for a generation of young people, many of whom emigrated and did not come back. And—here is the bitter irony—it did not even achieve its own stated aim efficiently, because cutting investment in a depressed economy suppresses the very growth that repairs the public finances. The countries that recovered fastest were not the ones that cut deepest. This time can be different, and the early signs, to be fair, have been different: the State stepped in at scale, wage supports prevented mass destitution, and borrowing costs are at historic lows. The question is what happens when the emergency passes and the bills are counted. If our future political leadership reaches reflexively for the old playbook, we will repeat the cycle: cuts, stagnation, social damage, political alienation. The alternative is to treat recovery as reconstruction—to invest in housing, health capacity, childcare and the green transition while money is cheap, to broaden the tax base fairly with those most able contributing most, and to grow our way to sustainability. So I ask every party in this House to say now, before the pressure comes, where they stand: never again austerity for those who can least afford it. The people carried this country through the pandemic. They must not be handed the bill for it twice.

One cannot fix what one has not mapped, and one cannot manage what one does not measure. It is an elementary principle of logistics, understood by every warehouse manager and dispatcher in this country, and yet apparently beyond the ambition of the government that presides over the whole network. Consider what we do not know, or at least what the government has never demonstrated it knows. Where are the chokepoints in our ports, and what is the actual dwell time of a container at each of them? Which rail corridors are at capacity, and what single points of failure—one bridge, one interchange, one labour dispute—can paralyze traffic across half the country? How exposed are our supply chains to disruptions abroad, and which critical goods—medical supplies, food inputs, semiconductors—lack any resilient alternative route? When the floods in British Columbia severed the road and rail links to our largest port, the government was as surprised as everyone else, and the response was improvised because there was no playbook to open. That is the cost of not mapping: every crisis is a novel crisis. What I am describing is not exotic. Businesses do it as a matter of survival; allied governments do it as a matter of policy. It would mean a national supply chain assessment, published and updated, covering every mode—marine, rail, trucking, air—and their interconnections. It would identify the bottlenecks, rank the vulnerabilities and attach to each a plan and a cost. It would give Parliament and industry a shared factual basis, so that infrastructure dollars flow to the constraints that actually bind rather than to the announcements that photograph best. And it would let us prepare for disruptions before they arrive, rather than striking a task force after the shelves are already empty. The pandemic and the floods were warnings, and the only question is whether we heed warnings or merely survive them. A serious government would have started this mapping years ago. The next best time is now, and if the minister will not begin it, he should explain to Canadians why flying blind is an acceptable transportation policy.

That is what is at stake in this debate, and I want the House to be very clear-eyed about it. When we talk about the post office network, we are not talking only about postage. We are talking about the pension collected in person by an older woman for whom that weekly transaction is also her social contact and, quietly, a welfare check—the postmaster notices when she does not appear. We are talking about social welfare payments, bill payments, banking services for people the banks have abandoned, and increasingly, as branches close across rural Ireland, the only counter service of any kind for miles. We are talking about the small business, like my own family's, that depends on An Post for parcels, for cash handling and for the daily rhythm of trade. And we are talking about postmasters themselves—self-employed, modestly rewarded, extraordinarily trusted—whose incomes have been squeezed to the point where many simply cannot continue, and whose offices, once closed, never reopen. The pattern is always the same: the closure is announced as temporary, the search for a new contractor quietly fails, and another community loses its centre. So the question for the Government is straightforward: do we believe the post office network is essential social infrastructure, or do we not? If we do—and every party in this House says it does—then it must be funded as infrastructure, not left to survive on a declining mails business. That means directing more Government services through the network, it means a public service obligation payment that recognises the social value the network delivers, and it means acting before closures rather than lamenting them afterwards. An Post has shown it can innovate and compete. What it cannot do is carry a public service mission on commercial revenues alone, and no fair-minded person should ask it to.

That episode should teach us something, but I want to be careful about what the lesson actually is, because there are members who would draw exactly the wrong one. The wrong lesson is that money to first nations communities is money wasted. That conclusion is not only false; it is a convenient alibi for doing nothing, and doing nothing has its own price, paid in boil-water advisories, in youth suicide, in children taken into care at rates that should shame this country. The right lesson is about accountability and capacity together—that funding must arrive through structures that ensure it reaches the people it is intended for, and that communities must be supported to build the governance, administrative and technical capacity that makes good stewardship possible. Those two things are not in tension; they are the same project. Where first nations have strong institutions—and there are many examples across this country of exceptional indigenous-led governance, in education authorities, in health services, in economic development corporations—outcomes improve dramatically and every dollar goes further. Where capacity has been eroded by a century of paternalism, by the Indian Act's micromanagement, by underfunded band offices asked to administer dozens of programs with a handful of staff, failures occur, and the same underfunding that caused the failure is then cited as the reason to withhold the remedy. So yes, let us insist on transparency—audited statements, published results, accountability flowing to community members first, because it is first nations families, not Ottawa, who are most wronged when funds are misdirected. But let us match that insistence with investment in the boring, essential machinery of self-government: financial administration, housing authorities, training for local managers. The communities asking for this are asking to be accountable. The honourable path is to fund the need and build the capacity together, and to retire, once and for all, the excuse that failure somewhere justifies neglect everywhere.

Those are not the words of activists chaining themselves to railings; they are the sober assessment of the world's assembled climate scientists and the head of the United Nations, and the question for this House is whether our policies match the language we so readily quote. I want to be constructive, because on the targets there is now broad agreement. We have committed to halving emissions this decade and to net zero by mid-century; the carbon budgets are in law. The gap—and it is a wide one—is between commitment and delivery, and it runs through every sector. In energy, our renewables ambition is real, but the planning and grid connection delays that stall wind and solar projects for years are a self-inflicted wound; a target without a timely consenting system is a press release. In transport, we are still building as though the car were the only future, while public transport outside our cities remains sparse and expensive, and the active travel budget, welcome as it is, is spent more slowly than it is announced. In agriculture, we ask a great deal rhetorically and provide too little practically: farmers are willing partners—I meet them, they are ahead of the politicians in many respects—but they need schemes that reward measurable outcomes, diversification support and honesty about land use, not blame from one side and complacency from the other. And in our homes, retrofit targets soar while the actual pace of deep retrofits crawls, constrained by workforce shortages we have known about for years and done too little to train for. So my ask today is not for new targets; we have targets in abundance. It is for delivery infrastructure: consenting reform with statutory timelines, a grid plan funded and published, a retrofit workforce strategy, and annual sectoral reporting to this House with variances explained. Code red demands the urgency of an emergency room, not the pace of a planning appeal. Our children will not ask us what we pledged. They will ask us what we did.

I want to speak up for those personnel and their families today, because the truth is that our Defence Forces have been living on their own goodwill for too long, and goodwill is not a sustainable pay policy. Pay, particularly for enlisted ranks in the early years, compares poorly with alternatives that ask far less. Allowances that recognise the unique demands of military life—the duties, the deployments, the unsocial hours that cannot be refused—have lagged. Accommodation on some installations is frankly not what we should ask anyone to live in. And underneath the material questions is one of respect: a sense among serving members that their loyalty has been taken for granted because, unlike others, they cannot strike and will not fail to parade. This Bill, and the wider programme it forms part of, begins to address that, and I welcome the commitments on pay structures, on the working time directive's application to the Defence Forces, and on the independent processes for personnel issues. The sea is our largest territory and our last commons, and the Bill before us will decide whether it is developed with communities or over their heads. Let me say first what I support. That is both unjust and foolish—unjust because these communities have fished those waters for generations and stand to lose access and livelihoods; foolish because projects that steamroll local knowledge end up in conflict, delay and the courts, which serves nobody, least of all the climate. Get this right and the offshore transition can carry our coastal communities with it. Get it wrong and we will spend the next twenty years fighting about it.

Madam Deputy Speaker, is it in order for a Member to characterise the diligence of others when the attendance record of his own Benches this afternoon speaks so eloquently for itself? I raise this not to score a point—though I confess the opportunity is not unwelcome—but because there is a serious issue beneath it. The currency of this House is presence and participation: listening to arguments one disagrees with, testing one's own case against interventions, and doing the unglamorous work of sitting through a debate rather than merely arriving for the cameras and the division bell. When Members treat debates as content for social media clips rather than deliberation—turning up, delivering three minutes of outrage to an empty Chamber, and departing before any reply can be made—something is lost that procedure alone cannot restore. My constituents watch these proceedings more than we sometimes imagine, and they notice the difference between a working Parliament and a performing one. I would also gently observe that the right hon. Gentleman's complaint about the time allocated to this debate would carry more force had his party used the time actually allocated. The Order Paper is not a menu from which one selects only the courses that photograph well. If an issue matters—and this one does, profoundly, to communities in every part of these islands—then it deserves Members' sustained attention, not their cameo appearances. So my question to you, Madam Deputy Speaker, is twofold: first, whether the Chair has any power to encourage Members who speak in a debate to remain for the wind-ups, as courtesy and convention have always required; and second, whether you will confirm for the record that the conventions of this House on attendance apply equally to those who lecture others on commitment. I suspect I know the answers, but the House benefits from hearing them stated from the Chair.

My concern, which I put directly to the Minister, is that the funding and the machinery are being asked to do several jobs at once and risk doing none of them well. Integration is not accommodation alone. It is English language provision, which remains oversubscribed everywhere I look. It is school places, and the educational psychologists and trauma support that children who have fled war demonstrably need. It is recognition of qualifications, so that the Ukrainian nurse or engineer can work as what she is rather than what the labour market finds convenient. It is mental health support, community sponsorship that is organised rather than improvised, and local authorities funded per person actually arriving—not per person forecast in a spreadsheet a year ago. So I ask the Minister for three assurances: that allocations under the fund will be uprated to reflect actual arrivals and published transparently; that support for one group of refugees will not be quietly financed by raiding provision for another, which would be both wrong and corrosive of public consent; and that multi-year certainty will be given to the councils and charities delivering this work, because six-month funding cycles build nothing. That is the issue at the heart of this debate, and I want to bring it down to cases, because policy abstractions hide what my constituents actually experience. Consider a parent whose child is receiving cancer treatment. The appointments are not occasional; they are daily or weekly, for months, at a hospital that may be many miles from home. Parking charges of several pounds a day, multiplied across a course of treatment, run into hundreds and sometimes thousands of pounds—levied on families at the most frightening moment of their lives, when one parent has often already given up work to be at that bedside. Or consider the dialysis patient who must attend three times a week, every week, indefinitely; the elderly husband visiting his wife on a stroke ward daily for months; the NHS nurse—and this is a particular scandal—who finishes a twelve-hour shift to find a parking charge notice on her windscreen because the staff car park was full when she arrived. These are not marginal cases; they are the routine reality of serious illness, and they amount to a charge on sickness itself—a tax collected disproportionately from the seriously ill, their families and the staff who care for them. I acknowledge what has been done: the concessions for certain groups are welcome so far as they go. But the experience on the ground is a patchwork—schemes that vary from trust to trust, concessions that must be discovered and claimed rather than applied automatically, reimbursement processes that defeat the very people they exist to help. A right that requires a healthy person's energy to claim is no right for the sick. So I support the calls made today: free parking for patients with long-term conditions, for regular visitors and for staff, applied automatically and consistently across the country. The money involved is modest against an NHS budget. The relief it would bring to families at their lowest point is anything but.

The persecution we are discussing should weigh on the conscience of the world. The evidence is no longer contested by any serious observer: hundreds of thousands of people detained without trial in camps their persecutors call schools; systematic surveillance that turns an entire region into an open-air prison; forced labour woven into supply chains that reach into our own shops and, if we are honest, our own homes; the suppression of language, faith and culture; and the measures directed at women, at birth and at family life, which sit within the definitions of the gravest crimes in international law. Faced with facts of this order, the question for a country like ours is never whether we can end the persecution by ourselves—we cannot—but whether we will do everything that is actually within our power. That is the standard against which I ask the Minister to measure the Government. Sanctions on the officials and entities responsible have begun, and I welcome them; they should be extended to all those credibly implicated, in concert with our allies, because coordinated measures bite far harder than solitary ones. On supply chains, warm guidance is not enough: companies profiting from forced labour should face legal obligations, with penalties, to demonstrate their supply chains are clean—and public procurement should lead by example, because the state should not buy what it condemns. At the United Nations and in every multilateral forum, we should organise, patiently and relentlessly, the widest possible coalition to demand unfettered access for independent investigators, because documentation is the foundation on which future accountability will stand. And we should support the diaspora communities in this country, who live with threats and transnational repression even here, and to whom we owe protection. History will ask what the free world did when it knew. Thanks to my hon. Friend, the knowing is beyond doubt. It is the doing that must now answer.

That is the economy we have built, and the crash in commodity prices has stripped away the last of the disguise. For decades, working people in resource communities have been told the same story: boom times are coming, tighten up during the bust, and whatever you do, do not ask where the profits from the last boom went. Well, we know where they went. They went into share buybacks and dividends, into executive compensation, into tax havens—everywhere, in short, except into the diversification, the value-added processing and the worker transition programs that would have prepared these communities for exactly the moment we are now living through. The workers did everything right. They showed up, they built the wealth, they paid their taxes, and when the price of oil collapsed, they discovered that the resilience was never built for them. Now, in the crisis, watch how quickly the rules change. When workers needed pharmacare, dental care or affordable housing, the cupboard was always bare and the fiscal anchors always binding. When large corporations needed liquidity, billions moved in days, with conditions so light they float. I do not oppose supporting employers through an emergency—jobs depend on it—but support without conditions is not economic policy; it is charity for those who need it least. Every public dollar flowing to a corporation should carry strings the public can see: keep workers on payroll, no buybacks, no dividends, no executive bonuses, and no access at all for companies structured through tax havens. That is not radical; other countries did precisely this. And when the emergency passes, the rebuilding must finally be the diversification we were promised: clean energy manufactured here, resources processed here, training for the workers whose skills built the last economy and can build the next one. The wealthy have had their bailout. It is long past time working Canadians got theirs.
