That is the contradiction at the heart of the position we are being asked to accept, and no amount of rhetorical fluency dissolves it. Let us walk through the logic calmly, because it withstands any scrutiny. All sides say they want no hard border on this island—London says it, Dublin says it, Brussels says it, and every party in the North says it. A border's character is determined by the degree of regulatory and customs divergence across it: where rules align, checks are unnecessary; where rules diverge, checks follow, whether we like it or not, because both the EU and the UK will protect their markets. Brexit, as defined by those pursuing it—leaving the customs union and the single market—creates divergence. Therefore, something must bridge the gap, either alignment maintained in some form, or infrastructure and checks. The backstop is simply that bridging mechanism reduced to writing: an insurance policy that applies only if and until a future relationship makes it unnecessary. To demand its removal while promising no hard border is to demand the outcome while destroying the means—it is to say the bridge is objectionable but the far bank must still be reached. I understand the political anxieties; an insurance policy with no unilateral exit feels, to some, like a trap. But the answer to that anxiety is to conclude the future relationship swiftly so that the backstop never operates, or to propose an alternative that delivers the same guarantee—and in all these months, no such alternative has survived five minutes of technical examination. Magical thinking about cameras and drones is not a customs regime. This is not about punishing anyone or trapping anyone. It is about the peace settlement, the daily lives of border communities, and an open border that people my age remember being closed. On that, there can be no gamble, and the backstop is nothing more, and nothing less, than the refusal to gamble.

All that is required is the will to lift it out. And while the Government hesitate, the gap in the law that the provision was designed to close remains open, and it is not an abstract gap: the people it affects are among the most vulnerable in our system, precisely those least equipped to wait through another legislative round trip. Each month of delay has a human cost that no one on the Treasury Bench has attempted to deny; indeed, Ministers have repeatedly accepted the case in principle, which makes the failure to act more perplexing, not less. So let me make the offer that my hon. Friend has made before, and add my name to it. If the Government bring forward the provision as an amendment in Committee or on Report, they will have support from these Benches and, I am confident, from all parts of the House; this is not a partisan question and never has been. If there is some genuine technical obstacle that has not yet been disclosed, then let the Minister set it out today, in terms, so that the House can judge it and, if possible, help solve it. What the House should not accept is the continuation of a vague assurance that the matter is under consideration—a phrase that has now been deployed across two Bills and three Ministers. The test of a Government's priorities is not what they say they support but what they schedule. This provision has been supported for a year. It is time it was scheduled.

It is the counsel of despair dressed up as sophistication, and it is designed to produce exactly the paralysis it predicts. The hon. Lady is right to name it, and this House should reject it explicitly. Notice how the argument works, because its structure is the same everywhere it appears. First, minimise: the problem is exaggerated, the evidence is uncertain, the victims are fewer than claimed. When minimising fails, deflect: others are worse, so why should we act first? When deflection fails, declare futility: whatever we do will be undone elsewhere, so any effort is wasted. Each step sounds worldly; together they form a machine for ensuring that nothing is ever anyone's responsibility at any time. And the extremes of left and right converge on it for their own reasons—one because action would validate institutions they wish to see fail, the other because action would constrain interests they exist to protect. The cynics' machine has only one weakness, and it is history. Every advance this Parliament has ever made was declared impossible by the sophisticated opinion of its day. The abolition of the slave trade was utopian meddling with economic necessity. The factory Acts would ruin industry. Votes for women would unravel society. Clean air, the health service, the smoking ban, the climate legislation of our own era—every one of them was preceded by confident voices explaining that nothing could be done, and every one of them was done. The people who did them were not naive; they were simply unwilling to accept that the difficulty of a task and the impossibility of a task are the same thing. So when we hear that argument again in this debate, from whatever quarter, let us call it what the hon. Lady called it: not analysis but anaesthetic. The task before us is hard. Hard is not impossible, and this House exists precisely for the hard things.
